name: Iris Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Seaview Medical Centre, in a seaside town where about a third of the people are over seventy. My mornings are mostly older patients with diabetes, heart failure, falls, and a long list of tablets each. Afternoons I do phone calls and two or three home visits. I'm still slow at sorting out who's on what medicine, so I double-check with Dr Abiola, my trainer, more than she'd probably like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the long-term patients. There's Mrs Dunmore, ninety-one, heart failure, who's told me her whole life story in fifteen-minute pieces over a year. What wears me out is the post from the hospital, forty letters a day to read and act on. My fiancé Daniel is a civil engineer at the council, designing road junctions, and we're getting married next summer, so most evenings are spreadsheets of guests and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible, really. Use the bits that help, like the tool that summarises hospital letters, and forget the rest. I'd probably say that at the practice meeting and leave it there, I'm not much of a poster online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's good news. My job is secure, and the town gets older every year, so there'll always be work at Seaview. Daniel's job is fine too, and with both our savings, the wedding and a house deposit both look doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the plan. Finish my training, get the wedding done next summer, and put the rest of the savings toward a deposit on a small house with a garden near the seafront. I'd use the letter summariser once it's been tested for a while, because forty letters a day is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, honestly, because we've got a lot of plans, and it's nice to think nothing big gets in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the forty letters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spotting the one that matters. Last month a single line at the bottom of a hospital letter said stop a blood thinner, and I nearly missed it. If any tool helps with that, I'll use it, but I'd want to see it catch that kind of line first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Seaview would be affected, even in this quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The secretaries who type and file the letters, a bit. There are three of them, and the summariser would cut some of their work. I'd guess one of them goes part-time, and that's real for her even if it's small for the rest of us.

say: It's **sensible**: use the bits that help and forget the rest.
The **letter summariser** is worth keeping, since we read forty letters a day.
think: My job is **secure** because the town gets older every year.
With both our **savings**, the wedding and a house deposit look doable.
do: Finish **specialist training** and hold the wedding next summer.
Put the remaining savings toward a **house deposit** near the seafront.
Use the **letter summariser** once it's been tested for a while.
feel: **Calm** and relieved that nothing big gets in the way of their plans.
S0.quote: Last month a single line at the bottom of a hospital letter said stop a blood thinner, and I nearly missed it.
fieldNote: Her life is full of **plans**: wedding, house and training.
She wants proof a tool catches the **one line that matters** before trusting it.
She notices small losses, like a **secretary going part-time**.

steps.text: Finish specialist training and hold the wedding next summer
Put the remaining savings toward a small house near the seafront
Start using the letter summariser once colleagues have tested it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's learn it properly and keep an eye on safety. At Seaview I'd ask for training sessions in work time, not evenings. With friends I'd be honest that I'm a bit nervous about Daniel's side more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own job feels fine. Old people with six conditions still need a doctor to sit with them, and that's most of my day. Daniel's job worries me more: a lot of what he does is drawings, calculations and checking, and his office has already started using AI to check designs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools once a couple of colleagues had them working, starting with the letter summariser and the prescription checker. Daniel and I would keep the wedding but trim it, maybe eighty guests instead of a hundred and twenty, and put the difference into savings. I'd want at least six months of both our costs covered before we buy the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for Daniel. My own work feels steady, but it's strange to think his might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel the night his office announced AI design checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're fine on my income if we have to be, and that he should learn the new system before anyone else in the office does. He's cautious like me, so I'd have to push a little. Then we'd look at the wedding spreadsheet again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said nothing gets in the way of your plans. Is that still true here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. The wedding still happens and the house still happens, but smaller and a bit later. That's the honest version: nothing gets cancelled, but everything gets trimmed.

say: AI is **coming anyway**, so let's learn it properly and watch safety.
Seaview should give us **training in work time**, not evenings.
think: My own job feels **fine**, because older patients with many conditions need a doctor.
**Daniel's job** worries me more, since his office already uses AI to check designs.
do: Learn the **letter summariser** and prescription checker once colleagues have them working.
Trim the wedding from **120 to 80 guests** and save the difference.
Cover **six months** of both our costs before buying the house.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly on Daniel's behalf rather than her own.
S1.quote: The wedding still happens and the house still happens, but smaller and a bit later.
fieldNote: Her worry sits with her **fiancé's engineering work**, not her own clinic job.
She trims plans rather than **cancelling** them, a typical steady response.
She'd **push Daniel** to learn the new tools first in his office.

steps.text: Learn the letter summariser and prescription checker after colleagues test them
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80
Build six months of both their costs before buying a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government needs to tell people what support there is, now. At the practice I'd say our older patients will need a human more than ever, because they won't cope with an AI on a phone. I'd keep it calm and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it frightens me for both of us. By 2028 the AI could do the thinking half of my job, the letters, the medicines, the diagnosis, and all of Daniel's design work. I'd still have the home visits and examinations until robots come around 2031, but I'd be twenty-nine and only half-trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my training toward care of older people and home visits, because that's hands-on and it's where Seaview will need people most. We'd shrink the wedding to family only at the registry office and put the house off, and I'd keep every bit of savings in the bank. I'd also tell Daniel to look at site work, like inspecting bridges, which gets the extra three years too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's a knot in my stomach thinking about two incomes at risk at once. But we've got savings and we'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's still happening, just small, and that we'd rather have a house in five years than a big party now. My mum would be disappointed, she's been planning flowers for a year. I'd tell my mum the wedding money is safer in the bank than in a marquee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your older patients will need a human. Is that what you believe, or what you'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, but I'm less sure privately. Some of them would love an AI that answers the phone at three in the morning. What they won't accept is a robot changing their dressing, and that's still three years off.

say: This is **too fast**, and government must explain the support now.
Older patients will need a **human doctor** more than ever.
think: AI could take the **thinking half** of my job and all of Daniel's design work.
I'd keep **home visits** until 2031, but I'd be half-trained at twenty-nine.
do: Move my training toward **care of older people** and home visits.
Shrink the wedding to **family only** and put the house off.
Push Daniel toward **site work**, like inspecting bridges, which lasts longer.
feel: **Anxious**, with a knot about two incomes at risk at once.
Steadied by **savings** and having a plan.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum the wedding money is safer in the bank than in a marquee.
fieldNote: Both household incomes are **exposed**, which drives her mood more than her own job.
She uses the **three-year robot gap** for herself and her fiancé.
She admits some older patients might **welcome** a night-time AI.

steps.text: Switch her training toward care of older people and home visits
Hold a family-only registry wedding and postpone the house
Keep all savings in the bank instead of a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, and practices should start training staff now. I'd ask at Seaview what the plan is for the secretaries and the receptionists, because they'd be hit first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years means I finish training and have a couple of years as a qualified doctor before it lands. I'd be thirty-two and specialised in older people, which is a lot of hands-on care until about 2034. Daniel has time to move toward site work, so I'm worried, but less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a diploma in care of older people alongside my training, over the next two years. I'd start using the AI tools properly once they've settled at Seaview, maybe in a year, so I'm comfortable with them by 2031. We'd keep the wedding as planned but smaller, and buy the house in 2028 with a shorter mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not anxious. It feels like there's a path. I'd still talk about it with Daniel more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a day at Seaview look like in 2031, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the AI reads all the letters and suggests the medicine changes, and I check them in half an hour instead of three. Then I spend the afternoon at people's houses, which is the part I like anyway. If the AI reads the hospital letters and I spend the afternoon in people's kitchens, that's not a bad trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Seaview?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three secretaries, mostly. By 2031 most of their work is gone. I'd want the practice to offer them training as care coordinators who visit patients, because they already know every family in town.

say: Five years is **short but workable** if practices start training now.
Seaview needs a plan for **secretaries and receptionists**, who'd be hit first.
think: I'd finish training and be **specialised in older people** by 2031.
Daniel has time to move to **site work**, so I'm worried, but less.
do: Take a **diploma** in care of **older people** over the next two years.
Start using the **AI tools** properly within a year.
Hold a smaller wedding and **buy the house** in 2028.
feel: **Uneasy rather than anxious**, because there's a clear path.
S3.quote: If the AI reads the hospital letters and I spend the afternoon in people's kitchens, that's not a bad trade.
fieldNote: She sees a fair **trade**: AI reads letters while she visits homes.
Five years gives both her and her fiancé time to **shift** toward hands-on work.
She wants secretaries retrained as **care coordinators**.

steps.text: Take a two-year diploma in care of older people
Start using Seaview's AI letter and medicine tools within a year
Buy the house in 2028 with a shorter mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well if people use it, and I'd say plan now, not in 2034. I'd keep saying it in practice meetings, calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the next few years, I think we'd be fine. I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, an established family doctor for older people, probably with a child or two. The bit that bothers me is the timing: we'd be in the middle of raising small kids when the thinking work goes, and robots come for the hands-on part around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned: training, wedding, house. We'd probably have our first child around 2029 rather than waiting, so they're at school before it all lands. And we'd save a bit more each year, so by 2036 we'd have two years of costs saved, not one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small worry in the background. It's the kids' timing that I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have children earlier rather than later in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather have the baby years while both our jobs are safe. If we wait, we'd have a newborn just as the thinking work goes. I'd rather have a baby's sleepless nights in 2030 than in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push Daniel to change anything with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, gently. I'd want him to move toward site work and project management over the next five years, the parts where you stand on a road in the rain. He'd grumble, but he'd do it if I made a spreadsheet.

say: Ten years is **enough** to do this well if we plan now.
I'd keep raising it **calmly** in practice meetings.
think: The **next few years** look fine for both of us.
The worry is **timing**: small children just as the thinking work goes.
do: Carry on with **training, wedding and house** as planned.
Have our **first child** around 2029 rather than waiting.
Save more each year to reach **two years** of costs by 2036.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a background worry about the children's timing.
S4.quote: I'd rather have a baby's sleepless nights in 2030 than in 2036.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her worry into **family timing** rather than job loss.
She'd bring children **forward** to have them while jobs are safe.
She manages her fiancé with **gentle pushes and spreadsheets**.

steps.text: Finish training and buy the house as planned
Plan the first child for around 2029 instead of later
Save toward two years of household costs by 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of my job alone, but because Daniel's and mine would both be hit in the same two years, just as we're starting out. What would help is clear support from the government, like paid retraining for people in their first years of a career, and a promise that home visits stay with real people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the household matters. Everyone asks about my job, but what keeps me awake is the two of us together. A household with two professional jobs sounds safe until both jobs turn out to be the same kind of thinking work.

headlineQuote: A household with two professional jobs sounds safe until both jobs turn out to be the same kind of thinking work.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old junior doctor** at Seaview, a clinic in a seaside town full of older patients.
She's **engaged to Daniel**, a council civil engineer, and they're planning a wedding and a house.
She's **steady**, waiting for tools to prove themselves, and trims plans rather than cancelling them.
Her mood peaks at **anxious** with two-year AGI, because both their thinking-heavy jobs would be hit together.
She leans toward **care of older people** and home visits, the hands-on part of her work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when her and her fiancé's jobs would be hit in the same two years.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** for people early in their careers.
A promise that **home visits** stay with real people.
